content: The timeline for conducting a costing study typically spans six months or longer. For smaller studies involving fewer than 10 sites, the process should take less than a year. However, a comprehensive costing study of all tuberculosis (TB) services in a nationally representative sample, such as those using the Value TB Costing Tool Suite and current TB guidelines, requires approximately one year to complete. The average budget for a Value TB study in one country, covering around 20 sites over 12 months, is approximately $100,000 USD. This budget excludes external technical support from the core research team and allocates about one-third of the funds for travel, training, and meetings, with the remainder covering staff costs. These staff costs include two co-principal investigators dedicating 5% and 10% of their time, a study coordinator working 10%, a data manager working 10%, and four research assistants or data collectors working 25% each for the year. Ethical approval is essential for costing studies, as they involve reviewing medical records and conducting staff interviews. If the costing study is part of a larger study that already has ethical approval, expedited approval may be sought, or the TB costing component can be included in the existing study’s ethical proposal. For standalone TB costing studies, ethical approval must be obtained from all relevant parties, which can take one to six months depending on the setting and whether patient records or observations are involved. This timeline should be factored into the overall study planning. In the case of the Value TB study, ethical approval was obtained from three institutions (London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, WHO Global TB Programme, and the Health Economics Unit at the University of Cape Town) and the medical ethical committees in five countries, such as Kenya’s Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI) and the WHO African Regional Office. Access to selected facilities was granted through permissions from the Ministry of Health at the county level and facility-level communications with managers, facilitated by the National TB Programmes (NTPs). Costing studies require a clear understanding of the production process for TB services. This involves defining the interventions to be costed, which may vary by setting and delivery mechanism. For example, TB interventions can occur at health facilities, through outreach programs, or at community or household levels. At the facility level, interventions may include vaccination, TB case detection and diagnosis, treatment, prevention, and infection control. Above the facility level, interventions may involve strategic planning, program reviews, training, procurement, and advocacy. Data collectors must assess the workflow of each facility, including how services are delivered, by whom, and the resources used. The costing process involves identifying and valuing inputs, which are broadly categorized into capital and recurrent costs. Capital costs include building space, vehicles, equipment, and training, while recurrent costs cover personnel, supplies, and drugs. Inputs for diagnostic testing and medication are added later, as these are more likely to change. Costing approaches include bottom-up and top-down methods. Both methods should ideally be used to capture a range of costs, from efficient practices to those reflecting real-world inefficiencies. The Value TB Costing Tool Suite, developed in Microsoft Excel with accompanying instructions, provides a standardized framework for costing TB interventions. It includes tools for data collection, data entry, and unit cost generation, as well as draft informed consent forms. The suite allows for the collection of both bottom-up and top-down data, including prices and quantities of resources such as staff time, training, building space, equipment, drugs, and supplies. The data entry tool enables analysts to clean and process data, generating unit costs for TB services using both methodologies. This tool suite can be adapted to various country settings and TB service delivery exercises.
